name: Kira Diaz

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. Everything you tell me stays confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm the office administrator at a vet practice in a small seaside town, three vets, four nurses and me in a back office that smells of dog shampoo. I run the appointment diary, send the vaccine reminders, file the pet insurance claims, order the drugs and do the staff rota. I use AI every day: it drafts the insurance letters and I check them, and I built a little system that sorts the reminder list for me.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the puzzle of fitting twenty-eight appointments into a day with one vet off sick. What wears me out is insurance companies, who lose forms on purpose, I swear. I live on my own in a studio flat, the pay's lower than a city practice, and after rent I've got about two weeks saved, so I watch every pound.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. I'll read it out. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a useful helper, nothing more, and people can relax. I'd probably post a few tips for other practice admins on the forum I'm on. I'd say the hype was silly but the tools are still handy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, not much changes, I already use the useful bits. The worry is money, because the practice was bought by a chain last year and they're looking hard at costs. A chain can decide to run the diary from head office whether AI is clever or not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using the tools and get even faster with the claims. I'd start doing a few hours of freelance admin for the dog groomer and the café on the seafront, because extra money is the only way my cushion grows. And I'd keep my head down with the chain's area manager.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. I'm confident in my work and nervous about my bank balance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why freelance work, rather than a better job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There isn't a better job round here, not in admin. The seafront businesses are all one or two people who hate paperwork. If I can do their bookings and invoices for a few hours a week, that's a hundred or two a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the chain need to do to make you worried?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Move the appointment line to a central call centre, which some chains have done. Then my job's half the size. I'd hear about it from the nurses before anyone told me officially.

say: I'd say AI is a **useful helper** and people can relax.
I'd post **tips** for other practice admins online.
think: I already use the **useful bits**, so little changes.
The worry is the **chain** that bought the practice and is cutting costs.
do: Get **faster** at insurance claims with the tools.
Keep my head down with the **area manager**.
feel: **Uneasy**, confident in the work and nervous about my balance.
S0.quote: I'm confident in my work and nervous about my bank balance.
fieldNote: Kira is a **daily AI user**, so the plateau barely touches her work.
Her pressure is the **new chain owner** and about two weeks of savings.
She reaches for a **side income** because local admin jobs are scarce.

steps.text: Use AI to speed up pet insurance claims
Do a few paid hours of admin for the seafront café and groomer
Keep running the practice diary and rota as normal

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. I'll read it out. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say be smart about it: use the tools, don't fear them, and push your employer to train you. I'd write about it on the forum, maybe a how-to. I'd also say chains need watching, because cost-cutting dressed up as progress isn't progress.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, a lot of my job goes. Booking, reminders, insurance letters, ordering, all on the card. The chain will want one central system with an AI answering the phones, and they'll keep one person at each practice to deal with crying owners and broken printers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to the practice manager and offer to run the new system for our branch and the two nearby. I'd grow the freelance side to five or six clients by the end of the year. And I'd look into a practice manager course online, because that's the job that stays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but buzzing a bit too. I like a problem I can actually work on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the chain let one person cover three branches?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They'd love it, it's cheaper. The question is whether it's me or someone they bring in. I'd want to have already proven it by the time they decide.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said a lot of your job goes. Doesn't that scare you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, a bit, because I've got two weeks of money and no one to fall back on. But scared makes me move, it doesn't make me freeze. I'd rather run around than sit still.

say: I'd tell people to **use the tools** and push for training.
I'd warn that **cost-cutting** dressed up as progress isn't progress.
think: Booking, reminders and **insurance letters** all go to software.
The chain keeps **one person** per practice for owners and printers.
do: Offer to run the **new system** for three branches.
Grow freelance work to **five or six clients**.
feel: **Anxious**, but buzzing a bit at a problem I can work on.
S1.quote: Scared makes me move, it doesn't make me freeze.
fieldNote: Kira expects to lose **much of her job** but moves first rather than waits.
She lives alone with **no fallback**, which makes the side income matter.
She is centre-minded: pro-tools, but **wary of the chain**.

steps.text: Offer to run the chain's new booking system for three branches
Grow freelance admin to five or six seafront clients
Start an online practice manager course
Learn the new phone and booking AI before it launches

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. I'll read it out. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is way too fast, and governments need to catch people, with income support while they retrain. I'd say it calmly but firmly. I'd tell other admins to start planning tonight, not next month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my admin work is gone by 2028, freelance included, because the café can just ask an AI. The vets and nurses keep going longer, because the hands-on work waits for robots, about three years later. So the only part of a vet practice that lasts is the part that touches animals.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the head nurse about training as a veterinary care assistant straight away. It's hands-on and the practice is always short. I'd cut to the bone and maybe get a lodger, or move into a shared flat to save rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'm usually the calm one and I wouldn't be.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is care assistant work something you'd want?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I've helped hold dogs for injections when we're short, and I didn't hate it. It's lower pay than admin, which is saying something. But the animals don't care how clever the computer is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you move out of your flat?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably, yes. My studio is half my wage. A room in a shared house would save me two hundred a month, and that's the difference between a cushion and nothing.

say: I'd call for **income support** while people retrain.
I'd tell other admins to **start planning tonight**.
I'd say it **calmly but firmly**, not as a scare story.
think: My admin and **freelance** work are gone by 2028.
Only the part of a vet practice that **touches animals** lasts.
do: Ask the head nurse about training as a **care assistant**.
Move into a **shared house** to save rent.
feel: **Alarmed**, though I'm usually the calm one.
S2.quote: The animals don't care how clever the computer is.
fieldNote: Kira sees **both incomes** go, her job and her freelance clients.
She moves towards **hands-on animal care**, using the three-year robot gap.
Rent is **half her wage**, so moving is her biggest money lever.

steps.text: Ask the head nurse about care assistant training
Start the veterinary care assistant course
Move into a shared house to save two hundred a month
Cut spending to rent, food and bills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called AGI by 2031. I'll read it out. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough if you start now. Use the tools, get a second skill, and don't wait for your employer to save you. I'd post that on the forum.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I've got time to do the practice manager role first, because that mixes people and systems. My admin work still goes by 2031. But a practice manager deals with staff and owners and complaints, which AI might take longer to do well.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd push for the practice manager job when ours retires in two years. I'd do the manager course now. And I'd keep a bit of freelance going while it lasts, saving all of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but in control. I've got a plan with steps in it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if AGI does management too, by 2031?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd be in trouble, yes. But managing a practice is half calming people down. A vet in tears after losing a dog needs a person, and I'd bet on that lasting longer than the booking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you save the freelance money for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A cushion, finally. Three months would change how I sleep. Right now one broken laptop wipes me out.

say: I'd say five years is enough if you **start now**.
I'd tell people not to **wait for employers** to save them.
think: The **practice manager** role mixes people and systems.
AI might take **longer** to handle staff, owners and complaints well.
do: Go for the **practice manager** job in two years.
feel: **Anxious**, but in control, with a plan in steps.
S3.quote: A vet in tears after losing a dog needs a person, and I'd bet on that lasting longer than the booking.
fieldNote: Kira bets on the **people side** of management outlasting admin.
She admits AGI could reach **management** too.
Her savings goal is **three months**, from about two weeks now.

steps.text: Finish the online practice manager course this year
Apply for the practice manager job when it opens
Keep a few freelance admin clients on the seafront
Save every freelance pound towards three months' cushion

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. I'll read it out. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty if people take it seriously. I'd tell everyone to learn the tools now and pick a direction. I'd also say government should make courses cheap.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years means I'm thirty-seven, and I'd probably be a practice manager by then anyway. I could even train as a vet nurse properly, which is a three-year course. I think I'd be fine, if I kept moving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the manager course and aim for the job. I'd look at the vet nurse course part-time later on. And I'd build the freelance side into a proper little business for a few years while it's still useful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Mostly hopeful, with a small voice saying don't get comfortable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why uneasy, rather than calm?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I've got no money behind me and I live alone. One bad year and I'm in trouble, AI or not. Ten years helps, but ten years doesn't fix my bank account.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to younger admins?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them to learn the people side of whatever job they're in. Machines do paperwork, but someone still has to calm down a person whose cat has died. That part isn't going anywhere fast.

I'd say government should make **courses cheap**.
think: At **thirty-seven** I'd likely be a practice manager.
I'd be fine if I **kept moving**.
I could even train properly as a **vet nurse**, a three-year course.
do: Do the **manager course** and aim for the job.
Look at a part-time **vet nurse** course later.
Build freelance admin into a **small business**.
feel: **Uneasy**, hopeful with a small voice saying don't get comfortable.
S4.quote: Ten years helps, but ten years doesn't fix my bank account.
fieldNote: Kira feels her **career path** is safe with ten years, so she eases to uneasy.
Living alone with **no savings** keeps a worry in place.

steps.text: Take the practice manager course and apply for the job
Turn freelance admin into a small registered business

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because my job and my freelance work go at the same time and I've got no one to fall back on. What would help is cheap courses for hands-on work, and some money while you retrain, so you're not choosing between rent and learning.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about people who live on their own. Everyone talks about families, but when it's just you, there's no second wage. I'm the whole safety net, and the net is two weeks wide.

headlineQuote: I'm the whole safety net, and the net is two weeks wide.
portrait: Kira is **27**, office administrator at a chain-owned vet practice in a seaside town, living alone in a studio.
She uses AI **every day** and moves fast, but has about **two weeks** saved.
She's **centre-minded**: pro-tools, but wary of the chain's cost-cutting.
She builds **freelance admin** on the side and aims for practice manager.
She's alarmed at two years but **uneasy** at ten, with a clear plan.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, losing her job and freelance work at once with no fallback.
whatWouldHelp: Money **while retraining**, so rent and learning don't compete.
